title: How to write a Claude skill?
subtitle: Structural and content patterns synthesized across the highest-rated Agent Skills in the corpus.
generated_note: Stats come from output/patterns.json (auto). Narrative is hand-curated.

sections.title: Read this first
sections.body:
A *skill* is a markdown file Claude loads to acquire a capability. People who write skills well treat them as **executable specs for Claude**, not documentation for humans. The patterns below come from analyzing 537 skills (after filtering templates and stubs) — the ones that consistently rank high on composite score share a small set of conventions you can copy directly.

The guide is biased toward **Agent Skills** (the dominant 78% of the corpus). Slash-Commands, Hooks, and Status Lines are simpler artifacts with their own shapes.

sections.title: 1. Frontmatter — keep it minimal
sections.body:
Two YAML fields are de-facto required: **`name`** and **`description`** (each appears in ~98% of serious skills). Everything else is optional and project-specific.

The other fields that show up frequently signal what kind of project you're in:

- **`allowed-tools`** — tells Claude exactly which tools to use. Common in skills that wrap a CLI.
- **`license`, `metadata`, `compatibility`, `author`** — appear together in skill collections that publish skills as a *catalog* (e.g., K-Dense-AI scientific skills). Useful if you're shipping a product, overkill for personal skills.
- **`argument-hint`** — used when the skill takes positional arguments (common in EveryInc's compound-engineering plugin).
- **`disable-model-invocation: true`** — when the skill is meant to run only when the user explicitly invokes it, not when Claude infers it's relevant.

Don't invent your own fields without a reason. Claude's loader ignores unknown fields silently, so they're cargo cult.

sections.title: 2. Description — write a discoverability trigger, not a tagline
sections.body:
The **description is the most important field you'll write**, because Claude uses it to decide *whether to load the skill at all*. The corpus splits into two clear patterns:

- **Short headline** (≤120 chars, 18% of skills) — works only when the skill name is already obvious. Example: `"Update the shipping address on an unfulfilled order before it ships."`
- **Long trigger** (>300 chars, 30%) — explicitly enumerates the situations and exact user phrases that should fire the skill. **50.3% of skills include an explicit `"Use when"` / `"When the user"` / `"Trigger on"` phrase.**

The winning pattern in the long form: state what the skill does, then list the cues that should activate it, including **direct quotes the user might say** (`"what's my thinking style"`, `"cognitive profile"`). This isn't filler — it's how the skill gets matched to user intent.

**Anti-pattern**: poetic descriptions that read like marketing copy. They don't help Claude trigger the skill.

exemplars.why: exemplary long trigger — enumerates intents + quoted phrases
good short headline — works because the name is unambiguous
balanced — explains the skill + when to use it in one paragraph

sections.title: 3. Body structure — the canonical 8 sections
sections.body:
The top skills aren't free-form essays. They follow a predictable section layout. Counting `##` headings across the corpus, these are the most common section labels:

1. **Overview** / **Purpose** / **Core concept** (>50%) — one-paragraph framing
2. **When to use this** (224 skills) — restates triggering conditions for the human reader
3. **Workflow steps** / **Steps** (109) — numbered, sequential
4. **Prerequisites** (113) — what must be true before running
5. **Parameters** (106) — usually a table when present
6. **Output format** (116) — sets expectations on what Claude produces
7. **Best practices** (275 — the single most common section!) — accumulated do/don't lessons
8. **Error handling** / **Safety** / **When NOT to use** — failure modes and out-of-scope cases

You don't need all eight. Pick the ones that fit. **A focused skill with sections 1, 2, 3 beats a sprawling skill with all eight.** The median skill has 18 headings total (`##` and below) — these are read as scannable cues, not prose.

exemplars.why: classic Overview → Principles → Workflow → Output structure
Purpose → Prerequisites → Parameters → Workflow — minimal but complete
domain-knowledge skill with section per framework

sections.title: 4. Length — aim for the median, not the maximum
sections.body:
The 537-skill sample distribution:

- **Body length**: median **7,000 chars** (~1,100 words). Half are between 4,900 and 12,800 chars.
- **Heading count**: median 18
- **Code blocks**: median 6

Very long skills (>20k chars) exist and rank well, but they're usually **multi-phase workflows** with internal sub-procedures, not just verbose. If your skill is shorter than ~600 chars, it's probably a stub or a description-only skill — Claude can't do much with it.

A practical sweet spot is **5–10k chars with 10–20 headings**. That gives Claude enough structure to navigate without burying the actual instructions.

exemplars.why: 19k chars — Anthropic's algorithmic-art uses length intentionally for examples

sections.title: 5. Formatting — heavy on lists and tables, almost always code
sections.body:
The corpus is **format-rich**:

- **99.6%** use bullet lists
- **93.3%** include at least one code block
- **79.5%** use numbered lists (mostly for sequential steps)
- **56.2%** include a table (typically for parameters, options matrices, or comparison)

This isn't decoration — it's how Claude parses intent. **Numbered steps say "do this in order"; bullet lists say "these are options or attributes"; tables say "this is a structured spec"**. Use them deliberately.

Commands and example invocations should be in fenced code blocks, never inline. Skills that put commands inline as backtick-`text` tend to be less reliably picked up by Claude as runnable code.

exemplars.why: parameter table + numbered workflow + code examples
heavy use of code blocks for diagram syntax

sections.title: 6. Trigger language belongs in the body too
sections.body:
Don't rely on the description alone. The strongest skills **restate trigger conditions inside the body**, usually in a dedicated `## When to use this` section. The pattern:

```
## When to use this
Use this skill when the user:
- says "X", "Y", or "Z"
- is doing <task>
- mentions <domain term>

## When NOT to use
- <out-of-scope case 1>
- <out-of-scope case 2>
```

The `When NOT to use` half is what separates good skills from great ones — it prevents the skill from being applied to adjacent-but-wrong situations. Only the top quartile of skills include explicit negative cases.

exemplars.why: elaborate When-to-use section with quoted user phrases

sections.title: 7. Naming — kebab-case verbs
sections.body:
Two naming styles dominate:

- **Verb-noun**: `clean-gone-branches`, `audit-codebase`, `analyze-competition` — for action skills
- **Domain-noun**: `competitive-landscape`, `clinical-decision-support`, `dhdna-profiler` — for knowledge-domain skills

Keep it **kebab-case, 2–4 words, lowercase**. Avoid clever names — Claude doesn't see the name first; it sees the description. The name is for humans browsing the file tree.

Project prefixes (`ce-*` in compound-engineering, `shopify-admin-*` in 40RTY) help group related skills in collections. Use them only if you're publishing a collection — they're noise in a personal `.claude/skills/`.

exemplars.why: kebab-case verb-noun, clear from the name what it does

sections.title: 8. Anti-patterns to avoid
sections.body:
From the bottom-ranked skills and shape outliers, these are common mistakes:

1. **Body < 600 chars** — skill is just the description with a stub. Either expand it or merge it into a sibling skill.
2. **No trigger language anywhere** — Claude can't tell when to invoke it. Adds 0 to the skill's actual utility.
3. **Description is a slogan** (e.g., `"The best skill for X"`). Useless for matching intent.
4. **One giant section** — no headings, just a wall of prose. Median skill has 18 headings; if yours has 1, you've lost the navigability advantage.
5. **Inventing frontmatter fields** — Claude ignores them silently. Stick to documented fields.
6. **Copying other people's skills verbatim** — common in the bottom quartile of newly-added skills. Easy to detect (duplicate bodies across repos) and contributes nothing.
7. **Templates checked into production** — leaving `{{your_thing_here}}` placeholders in the published skill. The `template` genre classifier exists in this corpus precisely because so many skills ship in this state.
